results.title: AI Code Review on GitHub: Copilot vs CodeRabbit vs an Agent That Reads Your Codebase
results.content:
Kenji tracked review times over three months. Average time-to-first-review dropped from 6.8 hours to 3.2 hours. Average review duration (time spent reading and commenting) dropped from 22 minutes to 14 minutes. PRs with zero reviewer comments on the first pass increased from 15% to 34%. The code didn't get worse. The automated pre-review caught the issues that would have generated those comments.

Anya's take after the comparison: "CodeRabbit is a good linter with opinions. The agent is a teammate who's read the whole codebase. I want both, for different reasons."

## Try These Agents [...] ## An Agent That Reads Your Codebase

The third approach was a PR template generator agent configured to review PRs against our actual codebase and team standards. The distinction matters: this agent has access to the full repository, not just the diff. It reads the existing code, understands the patterns in use, and evaluates the PR against what's already there.

We gave the agent three inputs for each review: the PR diff, the full contents of any files touched by the PR plus related files in the same module, and a document describing our team's coding standards and conventions. The conventions document included our architectural patterns, our error handling approach, our testing requirements, and our list of deprecated libraries and patterns. [...] The agent runs on PRs that touch core modules, APIs, or shared libraries. These are the PRs where pattern consistency and architectural compliance matter most. The agent's review takes longer, about three minutes versus CodeRabbit's 30 seconds, so we don't run it on every PR. For routine PRs like config changes or documentation updates, CodeRabbit alone is sufficient.

Human review still happens on every PR. The tools changed what the human reviewer focuses on. Before, reviewers spent time catching style issues, obvious bugs, and inconsistencies. Now, the automated layers handle most of that. The human reviewer focuses on design decisions, business logic correctness, and the question that no automated tool can answer: "Is this the right approach?"

## The Bottom Line: Your New AI Teammate

Building an AI code reviewer with the OpenAI Agents SDK isn’t just about automating mundane tasks. It’s about having an intelligent teammate that never gets tired, never misses obvious issues, and helps your team maintain higher code quality standards.

The best part? This agent works on any repository, in any language, and provides human-readable feedback that actually helps you become a better developer.

In less than 100 lines of Python, you now have a code reviewer that can analyze repositories more thoroughly than most human reviewers — and it’s available 24/7.

## Ready to Build Your Own?

The complete code is ready to run. Just grab an OpenAI API key, clone the implementation, and start reviewing your repositories with AI. [...] instructions = """  
You are a code review agent tasked with analyzing a GitHub repository.  
  
Your goals:  
1. Clone the repository provided in the user input.  
2. Inspect its contents to evaluate code quality, suggest refactoring, assess   
 documentation, identify security issues, and gauge test coverage.  
3. Use the tools at your disposal to navigate the repository:  
 - clone_repository(url) to clone the repo.  
 - list_files(dir, ext) to list files (optionally filtering by extension).  
 - read_file(path) to read file contents.  
4. After analysis, produce a concise report with separate sections for:  
 Code Quality, Refactoring, Documentation, Security, and Test Coverage.  
  
Provide actionable improvement suggestions for each area.  
"""  
  
agent = Agent( [...] """  
  
agent = Agent(  
 name="RepoReviewer",  
 model="gpt-4",  
 instructions=instructions,  
 tools=[clone_repository, list_files, read_file]  
)
The instructions work like a detailed job description. The clearer and more specific you are, the better your agent will perform.
